list.listitem: Oral contraceptives (OCs) can be safely initially provided to patients without a pelvic or breast examination. B

Combined OCs are a good choice for patients who need efficacy, reversibility, and safety; they should not be used in those older than 35 years who smoke, have migraines with aura, uncontrolled hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or acute DVT/PE or history of DVT/PE and not anticoagulated. The major risk factors with low dose pills containing <35 mcg EE are cardiovascular. B
Contraceptive failure rates are significantly lower with intrauterine devices (IUDs) and implants than with contraceptive pills, patches, and rings. B

Progestin-only contraceptives are a good choice for patients who are breast/chest feeding or have contraindications to estrogen, and patients who need efficacy, safety, or need to avoid estrogen-associated risks. C

High continuation rates at 24 months B and high efficacy A are noted with long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs—intrauterine devices and implants). Even if LARC are not used for the full period of efficacy, they are cost-saving in relationship to short-acting reversible contraceptives within three years. Higher initiation of LARC occurs with clinic training and public funding.

Emergency contraception (EC) should be considered up to 120 hours after unprotected intercourse or method use failure to prevent pregnancy; Self-administered EC is safe. EC methods include nonprescription levonorgestrel, prescription ulipristal acetate, and both copper and 52 mg levonorgestrel IUDs. B

Barrier methods are a good choice for patients with new partners or who have infrequent intercourse and are comfortable with use of the chosen method; they should be encouraged for those at risk of STI. C Spermicide should not be used for patients with increased risk of HIV. B

Many pregnancies occur when a contraceptive is stopped and another method is not instituted; patients should be counseled about anticipated side effects and encouraged to have a back-up plan if the initial method proves unsatisfactory and they are still wishing to avoid pregnancy. C

Research from the CHOICE project demonstrated that when counseling on contraceptive methods is provided and barriers to use, especially cost barriers, are removed there is increased use of the most effective contraceptives (LARCs) and decreased rates of unplanned pregnancies and abortion. B People should have "unhindered and affordable" access to all FDA-approved contraceptives.
Ninety-five percent of sexually-active patients with uteruses use contraception at some time during their life and, on average, each one uses up to three different methods.

Ninety percent of US patients with uteruses at risk for unintended pregnancy are using some form of contraception. Based on 2015 to 2017 data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 65.3% of women aged 15 to 49 years in the United States were currently using contraception. The most common methods reported were female sterilization (18.1%), oral contraceptive pills (14.0%), LARCs (10.4%), and the male condom (8.4%).

Eighty-five percent of sexually-active patients with uteruses, having intercourse with a partner capable of causing pregnancy, and are not using a contraceptive method will become pregnant within one year. The probability of conception is 15% to 33% per cycle depending upon the frequency of sexual intercourse. An ovum can be fertilized for only 12 to 24 hours following ovulation; sperm usually remain viable for 3 days after intercourse. Therefore, the most fertile period is several days prior to ovulation and ending 24 hours after ovulation.

Half of all pregnancies in the US are classified as unintended; about 40% of patients with an unintended pregnancy decide to have an abortion. Among teenagers, up to 75% of pregnancies are unintended. One reason for high rates of unintended pregnancy is a lack of contraceptive coverage by health insurance. For example, exclusion of Planned Parenthood affiliates from a state-funded replacement for a Medicaid fee-for-service program in Texas was associated with reductions in claims for long-acting, reversible contraceptives and injectable contraceptives, returned for a subsequent on-time contraceptive injection, and increased rate of childbirth covered by Medicaid. Patients also may not be aware of insurance coverage for contraception when it exists.
Other reasons for stopping contraceptives are side effects, difficulty with use, safety concerns, and lack of access to health care.

Contraception is the prevention of conception/pregnancy. Pregnancy is medically defined as the implantation of a blastocyst in the endometrium. Implantation occurs about 6 to 7 days after fertilization.

Assess risk of STI, need for maximal protection or permanence, perceptions of method risk, willingness to use a barrier method, and desire for spontaneity. Prior method success and failure will also influence choice.

Smoking: Estrogen containing methods are contraindicated in patients 35 years or older who smoke 15 or more cigarettes daily, and are advised against in patients under 35 years who smoke, or patients over 35 years who smoke less than 15 cigarettes daily.

OCs can be safely initially provided without a pelvic and breast examination; blood pressure measurement and review of medical history is adequate. Community pharmacists can safely screen patients for OC use, select appropriate products, and initiate OC use using collaborative practice protocols.
Contraindications to contraceptive methods are shown in .
Patients with uteruses 25 years and younger should be screened yearly for chlamydia A and gonorrhea. B
See for an overview of efficacy, benefits, harms, and cost of contraceptive methods.
See for important drug interactions with methods of contraception.
The Reproductive Health Access Project provides a series of "quick start algorithms" to guide the initation of various forms of hormonal contraception.

section.type: Combined Contraceptives (OC, Transdermal Patch, Vaginal Ring, Combined Injectables)
section.heading: Combined Contraceptives (OC, Transdermal Patch, Vaginal Ring, Combined Injectables)

list.listitem: Mechanism of action: Suppression of ovulation (primary), creation of thickened cervical mucus, inhibition of capacitation, interference with egg and sperm transport and endometrial changes that interfere with implantation.

Efficacy: OCs containing 20 to 50 mcg of ethinyl estradiol (EE), transdermal patch, and vaginal ring are equally effective (). Patients over 154 lbs may have higher failure rates from OCs containing <35 mcg of EE, so consider doses of 50 mcg EE for heavier patients. However, a large prospective trial of 58,674 women found few differences in OC efficacy for obese women, and only 1 of 5 studies in a Cochrane review found a higher pregnancy risk for overweight patients based on BMI.
A one-year vaginal ring (ethinyl estradiol and segesterone acetate) is available; adherence to this method is less when patients are removing the ring for washing or intercourse.

Taking an OC with a progestogen of long half-life (eg, drospirenone or norethindrone) for a cycle of 24 days plus 4 days vs. the standard 21 days plus 7 days regimen is associated with lower contraceptive failure rates (after 1 year: drosperinone-24 (2.1%), drosperinone-21 (2.8%), and all other (3.5%), respectively; after 3 years, 4.7%, 5.4%, and 6.7%, respectively).

Authors of a Cochrane review of 12 RCTs found no differences between traditional cycling of OCs (28-day) and extended (>28 of active hormone) or continuous cycles on contraceptive efficacy and safety profiles. Menstrual symptoms appeared fewer and bleeding patterns were either equivalent or improved with extended or continuous cycles over time
Contraceptive efficacy is not reduced when taken with non-rifamycin antibiotics.

Although pregnancy rates appear comparable, patients using OCs containing second-generation progestogens may be less likely to discontinue use than those using first-generation progestogens. Other reasons for stopping contraceptives are side effects, difficulty with use, safety concerns, and lack of access to health care. No male hormonal contraception is ready for clinical use.

Benefits: See . Lower risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer. Multiphasic products do not have an advantage with respect to side effects; monophasic pills should be considered as first-line agents. Three OC formulations (Seasonale, Seasonique [84/7], and Dolishale [365 days/year]; continuous) have extended dosing times with fewer "menstrual periods." Other agents are FDA-approved for the treatment of acne (Yasmin, Ortho-TriCyclen and Estrostep); agents that contain third generation progestins, low-dose norethindrone, or drospirenone have less androgenic effects and are also useful in preventing acne. Triphasic OCs have not been sufficiently studied to determine advantages and disadvantages. Authors of a Cochrane review found 6 placebo-controlled trials demonstrating the effectiveness of OCs in reducing inflammatory and non-inflammatory facial acne lesions with few important and consistent differences found between OC types. Based on 5 RCTs, OCs containing drospirenone 3 mg plus ethinyl estradiol 20 mcg may help treat premenstrual symptoms in patients with premenstrual dysphoric disorder, although placebo also had a large effect. It is unclear whether OCs are effective for endometriosis-related pain. Combined OCs are effectively used to treat hirsutism, sometimes adding an anti-androgen such as finasteride.

Adverse effects: Major adverse effects are similar for all forms of combined OCs and include stroke (1 additional ischemic stroke/year/24,000 current users), myocardial infarction (MI), venous thromboembolism (VTE) (1.5/10,000 patients/year), cervical cancer and breast cancer (mostly high-dose COC associated with a slight absolute risk increase). In one large Danish observational study, absolute risk was 24 thrombotic strokes and 13 MIs per 100,000 person-years. The risk of stroke among OC users increases with age and is considerably higher in patients aged 45 to 49 years than for younger patients. Nonfatal VTE is also 3-fold higher with OCs containing drospirenone versus levonorgestrel. The FDA has issued a "Black Box" warning advising against use of the transdermal patch in patients with a BMI greater than 30.

In a French study of almost 5 million, women, with a total of 5,443,916 person-years of OC use, stroke, pulmonary embolus (PE), and MI risk were all statistically lower with lower-dose estrogen (20 mcg vs. 30-40 mcg) and with use of levonorgestrel instead of desogestrel or gestodene. Overall risk of cardiovascular effects, however, was very low at approximately 6 events per 10,000 person-years.
OC use does not increase a patient's overall risk of cancer and may slightly decrease it. In addition, OCs do not appear to increase fracture risk, or cholelithiasis.

Limited data also show no major differences in carbohydrate metabolism between different hormonal contraceptives in patients without diabetes. Among patients with diabetes, there is insufficient evidence to assess whether hormone-containing contraceptives differ from non-hormonal contraceptives in diabetes control, lipid metabolism and complications. Use the lowest acceptable dose of estrogen to reduce the risk of these adverse effects.

Contraindications: A complete list of conditions where health risks likely outweigh the benefits of use or for which there are unacceptable health risks is available from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Contraindications include use by patients over age 35 years who smoke 15 or more cigarettes per day, patients with cardiovascular disease, patients with migraine headaches with aura or any patient over age 35 years with migraine, and patients with breast cancer, liver tumor, or liver cirrhosis.

Side effects: See . In the Cochrane review noted above, more patch users discontinued use compared to OC users, likely due to more side effects. Ring users had fewer adverse events than OC users but more vaginal irritation and discharge.

Drug interactions: See . In the single study examining outcomes, there were no significant differences in pregnancy rate (1.6 vs. 0.96 per 100 patients years for patients exposed to antibiotics vs. not) and overall failure rates were no higher than expected for OC users. For patients taking 20 to 35 mcg OCs who want to avoid any potential increased risk of pregnancy, short-term (3 weeks) use of a back-up method is suggested.

Key points for patient education: Counsel patients about symptoms of serious adverse effects (ACHES: Abdominal pain, Chest pain, Headache, Eye-problems, Severe leg pain). They should be advised to discontinue smoking, on how to manage missed pills and when to use EC. Apply patch to clean, dry skin of the abdomen, upper outer arms, buttocks or torso (not breasts). If it becomes detached, press it back on; if it does not adhere, replace with another patch immediately. Patients using the vaginal ring should keep the ring refrigerated until use; if expelled, rinse and reinsert. If more than 3 hours elapses, use a back-up method for 7 days. Vaginal tampons, antifungals and spermicides can all be used when the vaginal ring is in place. Providing patients of low-income with a 1-year supply of OCs (vs. 1- or 3-month supply) is associated with a significant reduction in unplanned pregnancies (1.2% vs. 2.9% for patients getting 1 pack and 3.3% for patients getting 3 packs) and abortions (0.18% vs. 0.63% for patients receiving 3 packs).

Mechanism of action: Thickens cervical mucus (primary action for progestin-only pill (POP) and may inhibit ovulation (primary action for DMPA and etonogestrel implant), inhibits capacitation, interferes with sperm and egg transport, causes endometrial changes that interfere with implantation.

Efficacy: See . The norethindrone POP does not suppress ovulation and the maintenance of a thickened cervical mucus is dependent upon dosing at the same time daily; therefore efficacy is impaired if the norethindrone containing POP is taken late. A drospirenone-containing progesterone-only pill, Slynd, is now available, and works primarily by suppression of ovulation. It has 24 active pills and 4 placebo pills (compared to all active pills for norethindrone). The Nexplanon implant (single-rod subdermal contraceptive) provides contraceptive action for 3 years. The implants have very high effectiveness. Following pregnancy, early (within 48 hours of delivery) vs. implant insertion at 6 weeks postpartum does not affect breastfed infants' weight at 12 months.

Benefits: See . These contraceptives are compatible with breast-feeding. POP and DMPA can be initiated beginning 6 weeks postpartum without adversely influencing lactation. In a RCT, there were no differences in lactation delay, failure, or continuation betweenwomen receiving the etonogestrel contraceptive implant within the first 3 days postpartum compared with insertion at 4 weeks (standard care); infants had no difference in weight at 12 months between early and conventional insertion timing . The contraceptive failure rate with implants is much lower than failure rates with contraceptive pills, patches, and rings and similar to DMPA. In one RCT among 510 patients following an abortion, the repeat abortion rate was significantly lower for those choosing DMPA than OCs (hazard ratio 0.55; 95% CI, 0.21-1.45). DMPA use is associated with a reduced risk of epithelial ovarian cancer (adjusted OR 0.52; 95% CI, 0.33-0.88) similar to OCs. Contraceptive implants can reduce pelvic pain associated with endometriosis.

Adverse effects: DMPA can decrease bone mineral density (BMD); this effect is usually reversible; based on two observational studies, however, DMPA users may have an increased fracture risk. Among DMPA users, BMD loss of at least 5% within 24 months is associated with smoking, low calcium intake, and nulliparity. Observational studies show no increased risk of MI with progestogen-only contraceptives.

Contraindications: POP, DMPA and Nexplanon should not be used in patients with breast cancer or history of breast cancer. POP are also contraindicated for patients with current DVT or PE, active hepatitis, severe cirrhosis, or benign/malignant liver tumors. DMPA should be used with caution for patients at increased risk for osteoporosis.

Side effects: Menstrual irregularity; most users of norethindrone and DMPA experience amenorrhea versus about 22% of implant users. Weight gain is common with DMPA (15 pounds over 4 years); however, authors of a Cochrane review of POCs found a weight gain of <2 kg for most studies up to 12 months. Weight gain did not differ at 3-months between patients randomized to levonorgestrel contraceptive implant vs. delayed insertion in one RCT. In a small follow-up study of 155 patients with an etonogestrel subdermal implant, 41.3% contacted a health care provider about implant-related issues after insertion and 25.2% (mean interval 9.8 months) requested removal (14.8% for bleeding changes). In a small RCT, use of 14 days of a combined OC vs. placebo reduced bothersome bleeding among etonogestrel implant users but bleeding resumed in 85.7% within 10 days after treatment. Tamoxifen, tranexamic acid, or doxycycline may also be used in select patients. A 2026 study explored the use of high dose oral norethidrone (10 mg daily) as needed for prolonged uterine bleeding associated with the etonogestrel implant. The study found the norethidrone group was more likely to have bleeding cessation and had fewer bleeding days, but a higher recurrence rate of bleeding compared to the placebo group.
Slynd may be more likely to lead to amenorrhea than norethindrone.
Implant insertion timing: Immediate postpartum (0-2 hours) insertion of the etonogestrel implant does not seem to impair lactogenesis when compared with later (24-48 hours) insertion .
Drug interactions: See . Although data are scarce, drug interactions are likely similar to OCs. There are no clinically-significant interactions for DMPA.

Key points for patient education: Patients should be counseled about potential effects on menstruation and weight (DMPA only). POPs must be taken daily at the same time each day; if more than 3 hours late, a back-up method should be used for 48 hours. Immediate-start DMPA is associated with fewer pregnancies. When DMPA is discontinued, it takes on average up to 10 months before pregnancy can occur. Rarely, removal of the implant is not possible and a contraceptive action would then continue beyond 3 years. Insertion of the etonogestrel contraceptive implant within 3 days postpartum (vs. standard 4 weeks postpartum insertion) was not associated with lactation delay, contraceptive failure, or discontinuation; patients who intended to use the implant were more likely to actually receive it when the insertion was done during their postpartum hospital stay.
Difficult implant removals : protocols for difficult implant removals exist, as well as algorithms for managing non-palpable implants.

section.type: Emergency Contraception (EC)- Levonorgestrel, Ulipristal Acetate, Copper IUD, and Yuzpe Regimen.
section.heading: Emergency Contraception (EC)- Levonorgestrel, Ulipristal Acetate, Copper IUD, and Yuzpe Regimen.

list.listitem: Mechanism of action: Prevention or delay of ovulation or fertilization (primary) and potential endometrial changes that interfere with implantation. Postovulatory events (eg, inhibition of implantation) have little if any role in its action. EC is not an abortifacient.

Efficacy: Highly dependent on timing. Use of Plan B One-Step, Next Choice One-Step, or My Way (containing levonorgestrel 1.5 mg single dose) within 120 hours reduces the likelihood of pregnancy by about 75% (89% if used within 72 hours). “Ella” (ulipristal 30 mg single dose) is also available and reduces pregnancy risk by 85%. Ella appears to be more effective than other drugs at >72 hours after unprotected intercourse. The 2 regimens of levonorgestrel (first levonorgestrel tablet followed 12 hours later by a second tablet or both tablets taken together) are equally effective. Use of OCs (Yuzpe regimen) within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse decreases likelihood of pregnancy by 75% but is the least effective regimen. When using an OC as an EC, use of 2 doses is necessary. Levonorgestrel EC may be significantly less effective in patients weighing more than 75 kg or with a BMI of 26, while ulipristal acetate may have decreased efficacy in patients with a BMI greater than 30. Doubling the dose of Levonorgestrel EC does not appear to increase its effectiveness in users with a BMI >30 and/or weight greater than 176 lbs.

ACOG recommends advance prescription of EC, although advance prescription versus conventional prescription does not decrease pregnancy rates. Increased EC availability is NOT associated with increased risky sexual practices (unprotected intercourse, multiple partners).

Mifepristone can also be used for EC. Authors of a Cochrane review of 115 trials conducted with 60,479 women, mostly in China, found high-quality evidence that all doses of mifepristone were superior to levonorgestrel (27 trials; RR 0.61; 95% CI, 0.45-0.83). Both mifepristone (3 trials; RR 0.14; 95% CI, 0.05-0.41) and levonorgestrel (6 trials; RR 0.57; 95% CI, 0.39-0.84) were more effective than the Yuzpe regimen in preventing pregnancy; pregnancy rates are estimated at 1-10/1000, 11-24/1000 and 29/1000, respectively. Ulipristal acetate (UPA) was associated with fewer pregnancies than levonorgestrel (2 trials; RR 0.59; 95% CI, 0.35-0.99).
ACOG recommends prescribing ulipristal acetate when possible over levonorgestrel due to greater efficacy up to 5 days.

Another EC option is the IUD; this device can be inserted up to 5 days following unprotected intercourse with an estimated pregnancy rate of ≤0.2%. The 2017 ACOG bulletin on emergency contraception recommends counseling patients that the IUD is the most effective form. The 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system is not inferior to the copper IUD for use up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse.

Side effects: Nausea (about 25% with levonorgestrel [Plan B, Next Choice, My Way] and 50% with Yuzpe regimen), vomiting (about 10% with levonorgestrel, 25% with Yuzpe regimen). No serious side effects. Patients using the Yuzpe EC should be advised to purchase a nonprescription antiemetic such as dimenhydrinate (Dramamine) or meclizine (Bonine) or be provided with a prescription for meclizine (Antivert) or another anti-emetic; NNT with meclizine (50 mg 1 hour prior to EC use) is 9 to prevent one patient from developing nausea.
Drug interactions: Information is limited; unlikely to occur.

Key points for patient education: Plan B One-Step is FDA-approved for nonprescription sale to anyone regardless of age. Next Choice One-Step and My Way are available to patients over age 17 years without a prescription. Ulipristal is only available by prescription and a pregnancy test is needed prior to use (unknown fetal effects). Because EC can delay ovulation, a patient may be at risk of pregnancy immediately following use of an EC; therefore, regular contraception should be initiated or continued after EC use. EC is less effective at pregnancy prevention than consistent use of other contraceptives.
This topic is reviewed in detail in a 2015 ACOG Practice Bulletin.

section.type: IUDs (intrauterine devices): Copper T380A (Paragard) and levonorgestrel IUDs (Mirena, Liletta, Kyleena, Skyla)
section.heading: IUDs (intrauterine devices): Copper T380A (Paragard) and levonorgestrel IUDs (Mirena, Liletta, Kyleena, Skyla)

list.listitem: Mechanism of action: prevention of sperm fertilizing the ovum (primary), creation of foreign-body reaction (endometrial leukocytes engulf sperm), altered tubal and uterine fluids that impair sperm function (T-380A). The LNG-IUS has hormonal effects such as thickening cervical mucus, inhibition of sperm capacitation, endometrial suppression, and may suppress ovulation.

Efficacy: See . IUDs are highly effective and long-acting (T-380A 10 years; LNG-IUS 3-5 years); long-term they are the most cost-effective contraceptives. Expulsion rates appear to be higher with insertion in the immediate postpartum period or immediately following abortion than with interval insertion; however, IUD use is higher at 6 months with immediate postabortion or post-cesarean insertion without increased complications. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis found the highest complete expulsion rates of 27% to 37% for placement of a LNG-IUD within the first 3 days after vaginal delivery. Expulsion rates were lower for placement of copper T-380A than LNG-IUS and after cesarian sections vs. vaginal deliveries.

Benefits: See . IUDs do not interfere with lactation and have no systemic side effects. The LNG-IUS can be beneficial for heavy menstrual bleeding. Ever use of an IUD is associated with a reduced risk for endometrial cancer: pooled OR 0.81; 95% CI, 0.74-0.90. The contraceptive failure rate with IUDs is much lower than failure rates with contraceptive pills, patches, and rings; in one cohort study of 9256 patients, the absolute difference was about 4 pregnancies per 100 patient-years of use. In one RCT among 510 patients following an abortion, the repeat abortion rate was significantly lower for patients choosing IUDs than OCs (hazard ratio 0.36; 95% CI, 0.17-0.77). LNG-IUD does not interfere with breast feeding. Cervical cancer may be up to one-third less frequent in IUD users. LNG-IUSs can also decrease severity of dysmenorrhea. Levonorgestrel-containing IUDs may reduce pelvic pain associated with endometriosis.

Insertion timing: Although expulsion rates were higher in the immediate postpartum group (>20% expulsion for 52 mg levonorgestrel IUDs placed less than 48 hours) compared to interval placement (no expulsions in patients whose IUD was placed 6-8 weeks postpartum), among the patients who had immediate postpartum IUDs that did not expel, the continuation rate was high. Placement at 48 hours post medication abortion appears safe and was preferred by patients and rated as less painful than placement 2-4 weeks after medication abortion.

In a recent RCT including 404 patients, the rate of complete expulsion of IUDs placed at 2 to 4 weeks postpartum was noninferior (within 6%) to placement at 6 to 8 weeks. IUD continuation at 6 months postpartum did not differ. However, the rate of partial expulsion after early placement was inferior. Shared decision-making should balance potential risk of pregnancy due to placement delay against this small difference in expulsion.

Adverse effects: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is uncommon and usually occurs within the first 20 days after insertion. In healthy patients, there is no need for prophylactic antibiotics at the time of insertion. A Contraindications are listed in .

Insertion pain may be reduced in some patients by using some lidocaine formulations, tramadol, or naproxen; lidocaine 2% gel, misoprostol, ketorolac, and most NSAIDs are ineffective. Nulliparous patients treated with 3.6 mL of 2% lidocaine intracervically had significantly less pain compared to sham-needling or no treatment.

Paracervical block using 20 mL 1% buffered lidocaine can be used to reduce overall insertion pain in nulliparous patients; scores on a visual analog scale in one RCT were significantly lower among patients receiving a cervical block compared to patients who received only minimal analgesia at the site of tenaculum placement (mean 33 mm vs. 47 mm on a 100-point scale).

Although use of naproxen does not reduce IUD insertion pain, it does reduce post-procedure pain. Self-administered vaginal lidocaine gel also does not reduce IUD-insertion pain but decreases pain with tenaculum placement.

Side effects: See . T-380A is associated with heavy menstrual bleeding and irregular bleeding during the first 3 to 6 months of use. In contrast the LNG-IUS suppresses the endometrium resulting in light irregular bleeding that ends after several months (20% experience amenorrhea). Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 studies found that bleeding or spotting requiring the use of sanitary products occurred for a mean of 36 of the first 90 days after insertion and then decreased markedly for most patients (to means of 19, 14, and 12 days in the 3 succeeding 90-day periods, respectively).

In one three arm RCT with 129 subjects, use of naproxen was associated with an approximately 10% reduction in bleeding/spotting days compared with placebo during the first 12 weeks after insertion of the LNG-IUS.
Drug interactions: None.

Key points for patient education: Expulsion is uncommon (2%-10% of patients) but more common among nulliparas and patients with severe dysmenorrhea. Patients should be instructed to check for the IUD strings and told to expect irregular bleeding or amenorrhea (LNG-IUS); amenorrhea is the most common reason patients discontinue the LNG-IUS. Use of an NSAID may be helpful to reduce bleeding and spotting days.

section.type: Barrier Methods (Diaphragm, Contraceptive Sponge, Male and Female Condoms)
section.heading: Barrier Methods (Diaphragm, Contraceptive Sponge, Male and Female Condoms)

list.listitem: Mechanism of action: Physical and/or chemical blockage of the passage of sperm into the uterus and upper reproductive tract.

Efficacy: Correct use is especially critical to the efficacy of these contraceptives. See . The contraceptive sponge is much less effective for patients who have given birth. In 2 U.S. trials, the 12-month cumulative life-table termination rates per 100 patients for overall pregnancy were 17.4 and 24.5 for the sponge and 12.8 and 10.9 for the diaphragm. Authors of a Cochrane review found that the Prentif cervical cap but not the FemCap was as effective as the diaphragm in preventing pregnancy. Combining use of 2 barrier methods (eg, condom with diaphragm or contraceptive sponge or use of a condom plus spermicide) significantly increases effectiveness. Condom features that minimize breakage are lubrication and receptacle ends. Polyurethane condoms are more prone to slippage and both polyurethane and synthetic elastomers are more prone to breakage than latex condoms, but typical use efficacy appears similar. Polyurethane condoms are an alternative for those with latex allergy. There is no greater contraceptive effectiveness for condoms lubricated with spermicide.

Benefits: All, except natural skin condoms, reduce the potential for transmission of STIs. Consistent use of condoms results in 80% reduction in HIV incidence. None expose a patient to hormonal effects.

Adverse effects: See . Use of the diaphragm with spermicide is contraindicated for patients who are at risk for or are HIV-infected. Repeated use of the spermicide nonoxynol-9 increases the risk of vaginal lesions and thus the risk for HIV transmission. (See Spermicides section.) For patients at high risk of HIV, spermicide should not be used with the diaphragm. Risk for toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is typically limited to patients who do not remove the diaphragm within 24 hours after insertion.

Side effects: See . Dermatitis associated with use of lubricated or spermicide-containing condoms may be eliminated by switching to another condom brand or type. Occasionally patients experience cramps or rectal pain from a diaphragm; sexual partners may experience penile pain. Sponge problems include difficult removal and vaginal dryness. Male condoms lubricated with spermicide are more expensive, have a shorter shelf-life, and are associated with a higher risk of urinary tract infection for female partners.

Drug interactions: Vaginal antifungals can rapidly damage latex condoms and reduce contraceptive effectiveness; use of latex condoms should be avoided until at least 3 days after use of a vaginal antifungal.

Diaphragm: 1 to 3 teaspoons full of spermicide is spread around the cup and rim of the diaphragm prior to insertion. Gels and jellies are preferred as they adhere to the device and are less easily diluted by cervical secretions. The diaphragm is inserted up to 6 hours prior to intercourse and must remain in place for at least 6 hours after intercourse; it should be removed within 24 hours of insertion. If more than one act of intercourse occurs, additional spermicide (any formulation) should be inserted vaginally; the diaphragm should remain in place.

Contraceptive sponge: The sponge is moistened with about 2 tablespoons of water, squeezed once, and then inserted so the dimple is pressed over the cervix. The sponge provides protection for 24 hours, can be inserted well before intercourse, and can be used for multiple acts of intercourse. It should remain in place for at least 6 hours following the last act of intercourse but should be removed within 30 hours after insertion; late removal can increase risk of TSS and result in a bad odor. The sponge cannot be used concurrently with a vaginal antifungal (dilution of spermicide).

Male condom: Apply over an erect penis. If the condom does not have receptacle end, leave about ½ inch space at tip to hold ejaculate; withdraw penis soon after ejaculation while still erect, holding condom to prevent slippage. Only water-based lubricants should be used with latex condoms. Avoid concurrent use of latex condoms and vaginal antifungals. Store in a cool dry location and use before expiration date.

Female condom: Insert one end into the vagina, near the cervix; the other/larger end lies outside the vagina partially covering the labia. Insertion can occur up to 8 hours prior to intercourse. Male and female condoms should not be used in combination (displacement of one or both). Female condoms are made of polyurethane which is unaffected by oil-based lubricants and vaginal antifungals.
Mechanism of action: Nonoxynol-9 is the chemical ingredient of spermicides; it is a surfactant that destroys the sperm cell membrane.

Efficacy: See . Use of an adequate amount of spermicide is necessary for contraceptive efficacy; foam products must be adequately shaken, and suppositories and films need time (15 minutes) to dissolve and disperse to be fully effective. A spermicide product with at least 100 mg of nonoxynol-9 should be used (lower doses less effective). When used as the sole method, contraceptive foams are preferred as the bubbles also provide a physical barrier.
Benefits: See . Can be used in conjunction with other contraceptives.
Adverse effects: Frequent (more than once daily) use may cause vaginal irritation increasing the risk of transmission of HIV and other STIs.
Side effects: Aesthetic concerns primarily (eg, messiness, leakage from vagina, taste); if irritation occurs, try switching to another product.
Drug interactions: Concurrent use of other vaginal products will dilute the spermicide and reduce contraceptive effectiveness.

Key points for patient education: Spermicides should be inserted close to the time of intercourse high into the vagina, near the cervix. Spermicides should not be inserted more than 1 hour prior to intercourse; additional spermicide should be inserted for each act of intercourse and douching should not occur for at least 6 hours after intercourse. Spermicides do not provide protection from STIs.

Although considered a "contraceptive gel" rather than spermicide, Phexxi is an intravaginal gel with typical-use effectiveness of 86% and perfect-use effectiveness of 93%. It is used by inserting an applicator of gel into the vagina up to 1 hour prior to intercourse. It must be reapplied for each new act of intercourse even if within the same hour. It may be used alone, or as a backup method with other contraceptives but should not be used with the vaginal ring.
Mechanism of action: These methods (symptothermal, calendar) depend on identifying days of the month when intercourse is most likely to result in pregnancy.

Efficacy: Cycle variability makes this method less effective. Authors of a Cochrane review were unable to determine comparative effectiveness due to poor study quality and lack of sustained use of these methods by couples.
Benefits: Minimal cost. Can also be used to promote conception.
Adverse effects and side effects: None.
Drug interactions: None.

Key points for patient education: Fertile days are identified using charted information on previous menstrual cycles, ideally one year. Fertile days are calculated by subtracting 18 from the length of the shortest cycle (first fertile day) and 11 days from the longest (last fertile day); abstinence or a contraceptive is used during the fertile days. Signs of ovulation: rise in basal body temperature (BBT) (a patient checks their BBT [with a BBT thermometer] each morning prior to getting out of bed) and cervical mucus changes (when mucus becomes slippery and clear [egg white appearance], a patient is entering the most fertile days). The safest days for intercourse are when cervical mucus is dry (between menses and first day of slippery mucus and after slippery mucus until start of menses) and/or fourth day after rise in BBT indicating ovulation.

Lactational amenorrhea: It is a contractive method of providing information and support to postpartum patients in how to use breastfeeding for contraception. Using this method, life table pregnancy rates at six months were reported in two controlled studies as 0.45% and 2.45%. The Cochrane authors note that similar life table pregnancy rates of 0.88% to 1.2% have been reported for fully breastfeeding/chestfeeding patients who were amenorrheic but not using any contraceptive method.

Recommendations for the optimal method should take into consideration life stage, couple preference, method effectiveness and cost. Younger patients should consider combining condoms with a hormonal method for maximal STI protection and pregnancy prevention or use of LARCs. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence includes the copper IUD and progestogen-only contraceptives (IUS, injectable contraceptives and subdermal implants) as LARCs and updated their guideline information in 2014. Data show that the etonogestrel implant and the LNG-IUS remain effective beyond their stated expiration date; the former was found in one study to have adequate hormone levels for ovulation suppression at the end of both 3 and 4 years of use and use of the LNG-IUS for a 6th year resulted in no additional pregnancies.
Authors of a systematic review of 12 studies, including one RCT, found high 12-month continuation rates (84.0%; 95% CI, 79%-89%) with LARCs among adolescents.

In one study, even among patients who come seeking short-acting reversible contraception, 43% were willing to be randomized to LARCs and 12-month continuation of LARC was high (77%) and higher than continuation of short-acting contraceptives—whether obtained following randomization or by preference.
ACOG endorses dual method use—condoms in combination with more effective contraceptive methods—to protect against STIs and unwanted pregnancy for adolescents.
Couples in a stable monogamous relationship with less frequent intercourse might considercondoms and/or vaginal barrier methods. Consider past successful use or failure of a method.
For patients with contraindications to estrogen and for lactating patients, consider POCs.
Condoms should be encouraged for those at risk of STIs. If maximal contraceptive protection is needed, consider addition of hormonal method or spermicide.

For patients post-partum, use of a LARC reduces the likelihood of a second pregnancy within 18 months compared to use of hormonal methods. For fully breastfeeding patients who are amenorrheic but not using any contraceptive method, life table pregnancy rates range from 0.88% to 1.2%. Menstruation rate at six months in all studies varied between 11.1% and 39.4% in this Cochrane review.

If permanence is desired, sterilization options should be discussed. Of female sterilization methods, electrocoagulation is associated with less morbidity including postoperative pain (vs. the modified Pomeroy and tubal ring methods) despite the risk of burns to the small bowel; studies were too small to determine differences in effectiveness.
If maximal protection is needed and permanence is not desired, LARCs (IUD, DMPA or implant (Nexplanon) should be considered the first option; OC use can also be considered.
LARC should be considered first-line for adolescents requesting contraception.
If maximal protection is not needed, options include barrier contraceptives, POCs, and natural family planning.

section.heading: Initiating Contraception and Managing Common Problems

list.listitem: Poor compliance and incorrect use are the most common reasons for failure of contraceptive methods. Brief counseling can reduce condom use errors. Combination educational/contraceptive-promoting interventions lower the risk of unintended pregnancy among adolescents, although this reduction was not statistically significant from cluster RCTs. Use of technology and social media to improve access to contraceptive information may enhance contraceptive knowledge and interest in LARC. Unfortunately, based on five small studies, behavioral interventions had little effect on increasing condom use among HIV-positive patients. Behavioral interventions were effective in reducing HIV and the incidence of STIs among female sex workers.

Providing provider training can improve initiation of LARCs. In a cluster RCT in 40 US reproductive health clinics, patients attending the 20 clinics randomized to receive evidence-based training on providing counseling and insertion of IUDs or progestin implants more often selected LARCs during the clinic visit (224 [28%] vs. 117 [17%]) and had a lower subsequent pregnancy rate among patients with uteruses attending family planning visits (hazard ratio 0.54; 95% CI, 0.34-0.85).

Many pregnancies occur when a contraceptive is stopped and another method is not instituted; patients should be counseled about anticipated side effects and their duration and be encouraged to have a back-up plan if the initial method proves unsatisfactory.

In a Cochrane review, half of postpartum counseling/educational interventions led to fewer repeat pregnancies or births or more contraceptive use; quality of evidence was low to moderate. Theory-based programs based on social cognitive theory or motivational interviewing were uniformly effective in improving short-term use of contraception. In another Cochrane review, community-based interventions (N = 3 trials), antenatal contraceptive counseling (N = 2 trials), and postnatal counseling (N = 1 trial) improved uptake of copper IUD contraception. In a database study, use of more effective methods was highest when contraceptive counseling was provided during both prenatal and postpartum time periods. In contrast, a counseling intervention did not increase use of a LARC following abortion; use of the LARC was high among both those receiving the intervention and controls.
Provision of free LARCs to adolescents and older patients is associated with high uptake and decreases in unintended pregnancies and abortions.

Opportunities should also be sought with men to discuss contraception. Based on the National Survey of Family Growth, 60% of male respondents were in need of family planning and, although most had access to care, less than 19% reported receiving family planning services, only 26% consistently used condoms, and only 41% had partners consistently using contraception.
See .

For most patients, the appropriate initial dose of EE is 20 to 35 mcg. Fifty microgram pills are rarely indicated (eg, patients taking enzyme-inducing medications, patients who experienced a pregnancy on a 35-mcg preparation, or patients for whom spotting or amenorrhea occurs with lower-dose pills despite altering progestin dose). Use of a generic, monophasic pill should be considered first. C

In addition to the traditional 28-day OCs (21 days of active pills; 21/7), there are extended-use preparations such as Seasonique and Dolishale. In addition, monophasic OCs can be given as 2 to 3 cycles of active pills given continuously followed by a week off for menses.

OCs are usually started at 1 of 3 times in the cycle—Quick Start (begin as soon as prescribed or after a negative pregnancy test is confirmed), First-day Start (begin on the first day of menses), or Sunday Start (begin on the first Sunday after the beginning of menses). One trial found no difference in pregnancy rates or continuation of use with Quick-Start versus First-day Start.

Typical problems are shown in . For breast tenderness or headache, consider decreasing the estrogen or progestin or both. For nausea, instruct the patient to take the OC with food or at bedtime or switch to a pill with less or no estrogen. If break through bleeding (BTB) occurs within the first 3 months, consider watchful waiting and discuss the possibility of missed pills or erratic timing. If BTB continues, provide a pill with higher progestin potency, a product containing a newer progestin, or increase the estrogen content or use a stepped estrogen product. Patients with amenorrhea can be reassured once pregnancy is ruled out or provided with a pill with higher progestin potency, a product with a newer progestin, or switch to a triphasic pill.

Problems include heavy periods, cramping, expulsion, and string problems. Heavy periods usually decrease over time but can be managed with NSAIDs during the first few days of menses. If persistent, check for pathology and anemia, and consider iron supplementation. Cramping is treated symptomatically if there is a normal examination and negative pregnancy test. If persistent, remove IUD. If fever and tenderness occur, consider PID, remove IUD, and treat appropriately (see chapter on PID). If partial expulsion occurs, the IUD can be removed and reinserted if desiret, giving doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours for 5 to 7 days. If the IUD string is missing, consider expulsion, confirm with ultrasound and consider reinsertion if desired. Long strings can result in partner discomfort and should be trimmed.

feature.caption: Contraindications to the Use of Contraceptives.
feature.feature_body:
Contraceptive Method Contraindication (Risk)
OCs • Breastfeeding <6 weeks postpartum (infant exposure to steroids)
• Breastfeeding 6 weeks to 6 months postpartum (decreased quantity of breast milk and duration of lactation)
• Smokers older than 35 years (thrombosis)
• CVD (HTN,* CHD, stroke) or high risk for CVD† (CVD events)
• Presence or history of DVT/PE (thrombosis)
• Major surgery with prolonged immobilization
• Thrombogenic mutations, such as Factor V Leiden (thrombosis)
• Migraine headache (with aura or older than 35 years) (stroke)
• Breast cancer (may worsen prognosis)
• DM with end stage organ involvement,‡ or with other vascular disease, or if >20 years duration (CVD and thrombosis)
• Gall bladder disease (worsening)
• Liver disease, such as viral hepatitis, cirrhosis, tumor (worsen prognosis, increase tumor size)
Progestin-only contraceptives (POCs) • Breastfeeding <6 weeks postpartum (theoretical concerns; ie, once breastfeeding is well established, POCs do not have any negative effect on volume or quality of milk)
Progestin-only pill • Bone density (decreased with DMPA; reversible on discontinuing)
DMPA • CVD (CHD, stroke) or high risk for CVD† (all POCs); HTN* (DMPA increased CVD events)
Etonogestrel implant • Presence of DVT/PE (thrombosis—DMPA)
• Migraine headache with focal neurologic symptoms (stroke—all POC)
• Breast cancer (may worsen prognosis)
• DM as above (CVD and thrombosis—all POCs)
• Liver disease, such as viral hepatitis, cirrhosis, tumor (worsen prognosis, increase tumor size—all POCs)
IUD • Postpartum (<48 hours perhaps up to 4 months) (increased expulsion rate)
• Distorted uterine cavity; fibroids (difficult placement)
• Active or recurrent pelvic infection (worsen condition)
• STI (current or within 3 months) or at high risk of STI (increased risk of PID)
• Presence of DVT/PE (LNG-IUS—thrombosis)
• Migraine headache with focal neurologic symptoms (LNG-IUS—stroke, worsen migraine)
• Liver disease, such as viral hepatitis, cirrhosis, tumor (LNG-IUS—worsen prognosis, increase tumor size)
Barrier Methods (diaphragm, contraceptive sponge, male condom, female condom) • Latex allergy (diaphragm, some male condoms) or spermicide allergy
• Abnormal vaginal anatomy or uterine prolapse
• History of toxic shock syndrome or UTI (except female condom)
• Inability of patient to place or remove
Abbreviations: CHD, coronary heart disease; CVD, cardiovascular disease; DM, diabetes mellitus; DVT, deep venous thrombosis; HTN, hypertension. LNG-IUS, levonorgestrel intrauterine system; MI, myocardial infarction; OC, oral contraceptive; PE, pulmonary embolism; PID, pelvic inflammatory disease; STI, sexually transmitted infection.*Women with controlled HTN are at less risk for CVD events than women with untreated HTN. †Multiple risk factors such as age, smoking, DM, HTN. ‡nephropathy, neuropathy, retinopathy.

feature.caption: Selected Clinically Significant Interactions with Oral Contraceptives.*
feature.feature_body:
Drug Interaction Management Recommendation
May reduce the efficacy of oral contraceptives
Antibiotics (ie, penicillins, tetracyclines) Reduced efficacy unlikely; contraceptive failure may be a possibility in a very small percentage of women. For women taking a 20 mcg to 35 mcg OC who wish to avoid any possible increase in pregnancy risk, use back-up method during antibiotic therapy or for 14 days (whichever is shorter) plus 7 days.
Aprepitant, bosentan, felbamate, griseofulvin, hydantoins (eg, phenytoin, mephenytoin, ethotoin), modafinil, nevirapine, protease inhibitors (nelfinavir, ritonavir, lopinavir, tipranavir), rifampin, St. John's wort Use an alternative contraceptive or an additional nonhormonal back-up method during concurrent therapy. For aprepitant and modafinil, use a nonhormonal back-up method and continue for at least 1 month after stopping therapy.
Barbiturates, carbamazepine, primidone, oxcarbazepine, topiramate Use an alternative contraceptive or a higher estrogen dose OC (titrate estrogen dose to avoid breakthrough bleeding) during concurrent therapy.
Bexarotene, isotretinoin Use more than one method of contraception concurrently during the use of retinoids (bexarotene, isotretinoin). One method of contraception should be nonhormonal.
OCs may increase adverse effects and toxicity
Cyclosporine, troleandomycin Avoid concurrent use.
Alprazolam (and perhaps other benzodiazepines), prednisone, methylprednisolone, selegiline, theophylline, tizanidine Monitor for adverse effects and reduce the dose as needed.
Other interactions
Lamotrigine Potential decreased effect of lamotrigine; adjust dose as needed.
Licorice (herbal) Interaction is possible with herbal licorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra). Potential for elevated blood pressure and fluid retention; monitor blood pressure and stop licorice use if it increases.
Red clover Possible loss of contraceptive efficacy or increased estrogen toxicity; avoid concurrent use.
Caffeine Possible increased CNS stimulation; decrease caffeine intake if this occurs.
*Also presumed to occur with the progestin-only pill, etonogestrel implant, transdermal patch, and vaginal ring. Adapted from Shimp LA. Contraception. 2006;(April):1-8.
